title: Cervical Screening Test (Renewed NCSP) - Counselling and Result Interpretation
patient_instructions: You are Jessica Barton, a 32-year-old graphic designer, who has come to discuss your cervical screening. Default scenario (result interpretation): you did a cervical screening test and have returned for the result. You are anxious and say 'My mum had Pap smears, this is all new and I'm worried something is wrong.' Your result is HPV 16 positive, cytology normal. You have had multiple partners in the past, do not always use condoms, are on the pill, and never had the Gardasil vaccine because you are afraid of needles. You have no symptoms - no bleeding, no pain, no discharge. If the assigned scenario is 'counselling about the new program', you received a reminder letter and want to understand why screening changed from the old Pap smear and what happens during the test; you are nervous about a speculum examination and would like to know your options. Affect: worried, asks lots of questions. Only reveal the HPV 16 result concern and your vaccination/needle-phobia history when the candidate explores them.
candidate_instructions: Setting: General practice. Jessica Barton, 32, attends to discuss cervical screening. In the next 8 minutes: briefly clarify her history and concerns, then counsel her about the renewed National Cervical Screening Program and, if a result is provided, interpret it and explain the next step. Explain the procedure and offer self-collection. Check her understanding throughout. No examination is required.
examiner_instructions: Look for clear, patient-centred counselling. The candidate should explain that the program now tests for HPV first (the cause of almost all cervical cancer), screens 25-74 years, is 5-yearly, and that reflex liquid-based cytology is done only if HPV is detected. For the result scenario, the candidate must interpret HPV 16 positive with normal cytology correctly: HPV 16/18 = higher-risk, refer for colposcopy regardless of cytology; reassure that normal cytology means no cell changes yet, and that this is not cancer. They should offer and correctly describe self-collection: a self-collected vaginal sample is AS ACCURATE as clinician-collected for detecting oncogenic HPV; the only limitation is it cannot have reflex cytology, so an HPV-positive non-16/18 self-collection needs a follow-up clinician-collected sample. Do NOT accept 'self-collection is less accurate'. Emphasise symptomatic patients need a co-test, not screening. Prompt if needed: 'How accurate is self-collection compared with clinician collection?'

criteria: Opens with agenda-setting and elicits her specific concern and prior understanding
Takes relevant cervix history: previous screening, Gardasil status, family/personal cervical history, symptoms
Screens for symptoms that would mandate a co-test rather than screening (PCB, abnormal discharge/bleeding)
Explores contraception and risk factors without inappropriately advising cessation of an effective contraceptive
Correctly interprets the provided result (HPV 16 positive + normal cytology = colposcopy regardless of cytology)
Explains the intermediate-risk pathway (HPV non-16/18 with normal/LSIL = repeat HPV in 12 months)
Distinguishes screening (asymptomatic) from a co-test for symptomatic patients
Refers appropriately for colposcopy and explains what a colposcopy involves in lay terms
Offers self-collection and states correctly it is as accurate as clinician-collection for HPV (limitation is no reflex cytology)
Safety-nets: symptomatic bleeding needs examination/co-test; post-menopausal bleeding additionally needs TV ultrasound +/- endometrial sampling
Uses plain language, checks understanding, manages anxiety and avoids jargon
Documents consent/chaperone offer and that self-collection was offered

red_flags: Symptomatic patients (post-coital, intermenstrual or post-menopausal bleeding, persistent unexplained discharge) require a co-test, not routine screening - non-menstrual bleeding is cancer until proven otherwise
HPV 16/18 detected on screening warrants colposcopy referral regardless of cytology result
A cervix that is ulcerated, friable or bleeds readily on contact indicates possible cervical cancer and warrants urgent gynaecological referral
Post-menopausal bleeding additionally mandates transvaginal ultrasound +/- endometrial sampling (endometrial cancer until proven otherwise)
australian_guidelines: National Cervical Screening Program (renewed NCSP): primary HPV test 5-yearly for people with a cervix aged 25-74 (exit test 70-74); reflex liquid-based cytology performed only if oncogenic HPV detected

NCSP self-collection (universal eligibility from 1 July 2022): a self-collected vaginal sample is as accurate as a clinician-collected sample for detecting oncogenic HPV; the limitation is it cannot undergo reflex cytology, so HPV-positive non-16/18 self-collection needs a follow-up clinician-collected sample
NCSP risk pathways: HPV 16/18 positive = higher risk, refer to colposcopy regardless of cytology; HPV non-16/18 with normal/LSIL = repeat HPV in 12 months; HSIL or persistent HPV = colposcopy
RACGP/NCSP: symptomatic patients require a co-test (HPV plus cytology together, requested regardless of HPV result), examination of the cervix and consideration of colposcopy/referral
learning_objectives: Counsel a patient on the rationale and structure of the renewed HPV-based NCSP
Interpret CST results and apply the correct risk-based management pathway
Offer and accurately describe self-collection as an evidence-based, equally accurate option
key_points: HPV causes almost all cervical cancer and precedes cell changes by 10-15 years, making 5-yearly HPV testing safe and effective
LSIL/HSIL are precancerous changes, not cancer - reassure accordingly
First CST at age 25 with an exit test between 70-74 years
Asymptomatic ectropion needs reassurance only; do not routinely cease effective contraception

citations.claim: LSIL and HSIL are cytological/histological grades (CIN1 = LSIL and CIN2-3/CIS = HSIL) representing precancerous changes, not cancer, supporting reassurance that these are not yet cancer.
citations.source: John Murtagh General Practice, 8th Edition.pdf (Australian modified Bethesda System, p. 2457)

citations.claim: It is vital that cells are taken from the cervical transformation zone in screening, supporting speculum technique and the limitation that self-collected vaginal samples do not sample the transformation zone for cytology.
citations.source: John Murtagh General Practice, 8th Edition.pdf (transformation zone, p. 2455)

citations.claim: Non-menstrual bleeding (post-coital, intermenstrual, post-menopausal) suggests cancer until proven otherwise and requires referral, supporting the co-test/investigation pathway for symptomatic patients.
citations.source: John Murtagh General Practice, 8th Edition.pdf (when to refer, p. 2550)

citations.claim: A cervix that is ulcerated, friable or bleeds readily on contact indicates cervical cancer and warrants urgent gynaecological referral.
citations.source: John Murtagh General Practice, 8th Edition.pdf (cervical cancer examination, p. 2547)
